items.title: Media executive calls for greater cooperation, human oversight in AI-driven journalism
text: ISTANBUL, Nov. 7 (Xinhua) -- Artificial intelligence (AI) is opening up new possibilities for journalism, but media organizations must strengthen cooperation to ensure technological advances go hand in hand with reliable reporting, said Sumeyra Teymur, CEO of Turkish news platform Haberler.com.

In an interview ahead of the 7th World Media Summit, Teymur praised China's innovative use of AI in journalism, saying she was impressed by the country's efforts to integrate advanced technologies into the media industry.

"I heard about and saw AI anchors presenting news during my previous visit, which really impressed me," she said. "I have always loved technology, and these developments make me excited. I am always thinking about what is coming next."
She also expressed interest in the potential use of humanoid robots to cover dangerous situations, such as earthquakes and conflicts, where deploying human reporters could pose risks.

Haberler.com has also integrated AI into its daily operations. Receiving more than 2,000 news articles from various sources every day, the platform uses AI to organize content, generate headlines and supplement articles with relevant photos and videos, enabling its editorial team to handle a larger volume of news.

However, Teymur stressed that human oversight remains essential, warning that AI can make mistakes and facilitate the creation of fabricated news, images and videos, as well as the manipulation of voices and identities.
"Whenever we use AI, we always have a human checking the content," she said, emphasizing the responsibility of media organizations to verify information before publication.

She called for stronger international media cooperation in sharing information, technological expertise and cultural stories, noting that no single organization can tackle the rapid spread of misinformation across borders alone.

The 7th World Media Summit, hosted by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing Municipal People's Government under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action," is being held in Beijing from Nov. 5 to 9.
Teymur said she looked forward to exchanging experience with Chinese journalists and strengthening ties with Chinese media organizations.  ■

items.title: Xinhua Middle East news summary at 2200 GMT, Nov. 6
text: SANAA -- At least 30 people were killed and eight others wounded in an attack on a crowded market in Yemen's southwestern Taiz province on Friday, Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported, as the country's government and Houthi group traded accusations over responsibility.

The channel said three Saudi airstrikes hit Al-Hadarah public market in Taiz's Al-Wazi'iyah district in the morning, when it was crowded with shoppers. The casualty toll remained preliminary as rescue teams continued searching through the rubble, it added. (Yemen-Attack-Casuality)

JERUSALEM -- The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday issued its first response to U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement that Washington will end its annual military aid to Israel, saying that Israel and the United States agreed to move from military aid to partnership.

"U.S. military aid to Israel has always been a cross-the-aisle agreement," Netanyahu said in the statement. "Israel has used it both to defend itself and to confront enemies who threaten America and the West." (Israel-US-Military Aid)

TEHRAN -- A senior Iranian security official said on Friday that Iran needs to see practical measures by the United States rather than mere "paper commitments" before entering a new phase of diplomacy.

"It is Iran's right not to settle for the U.S. paper commitments for entering a new phase of diplomacy. We need to see practical measures from the Americans, actions that are quite self-evident," Deputy Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Ali Bagheri Kani said in an interview with state-run IRIB TV. (Iran-US-Diplomacy)

DOHA -- Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and U.S. President Donald Trump discussed ongoing diplomatic efforts to ease regional tensions and reach a comprehensive agreement to end the crisis during a phone call on Friday, Qatar's Emiri Diwan, the administrative office of the emir, said.

They reviewed the latest regional developments, particularly Qatar's mediation efforts to narrow differences between the parties concerned and support negotiations toward a lasting settlement, according to a statement from the Emiri Diwan. (Qatar-US-Diplomacy)  ■

items.title: Eastern DRC violence claims lives, disrupts Ebola response: UN
text: UNITED NATIONS, Nov. 6 (Xinhua) -- Dozens of civilians were reportedly killed overnight in violence in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), further disrupting the Ebola response, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said Friday.

At least 30 civilians were killed, homes were burned and a health center was destroyed in the Cantine-Aloya locality of Beni Territory in North Kivu. Several patients are reportedly among the dead, the office said, citing local sources.

"People who had been in contact with Ebola patients reportedly fled an observation centre, while response teams were forced to suspend operations in the area," the office said in a daily news update. "This is making it harder to track potential infections and contain the outbreak."
Authorities have reported more than 10,700 confirmed Ebola cases and over 5,200 deaths to date, mainly in the eastern DRC, according to OCHA.
The office calls on all parties in the country to protect civilians, respect international humanitarian law and ensure safe and unhindered access for humanitarian and health workers.  ■

items.title: 10 civilians killed in suspected ADF attack in eastern DR Congo: local sources
text: Photo taken on Nov. 6, 2026 shows the debris after an attack in Cantine-Aloya, a locality in Beni territory, North Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). At least 10 civilians were killed and several houses were set ablaze in an overnight attack by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), local media reported Friday, citing civil society sources. (Xinhua)

KINSHASA, Nov. 6 (Xinhua) -- At least 10 civilians were killed and several houses were set ablaze in an overnight attack by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), local media reported Friday, citing civil society sources.

The attack occurred overnight from Thursday into Friday in Cantine-Aloya, a locality in Beni territory, North Kivu province. Armed assailants reportedly entered the settlement, killing residents and setting fire to homes and commercial buildings.
Tchetche Aliamini, head of a local civil society organization, confirmed the attack and reported extensive damage to civilian property, according to local media.

The death toll remains provisional, with some local media outlets reporting that more than 20 people were killed. Some bodies were reportedly still at the scene, while many residents fled their homes amid the violence.

The ADF, an affiliate of the Islamic State in Central Africa, is a Ugandan rebel group operating in eastern DRC. Its continued activity has prompted joint military operations by Congolese and Ugandan forces since November 2021 to track down and neutralize the group. ■

Construction workers, truck driver injured as section of bridge collapses
text: Three construction workers and one passing truck driver were injured on Saturday after a section of a bridge collapsed during the jacking of a steel truss at the construction site for the Cangzhou-Yulin Expressway, according to authorities.
The construction site was located in the Qingyuan district of Baoding, Hebei province, crossing the expressway linking Cangzhou, Hebei, and Yulin, Shaanxi province.
Two of the construction workers sustained serious injuries. All the injured have been promptly taken to the hospital for treatment.

Currently, local authorities are working on-site to ensure that the expressway can resume traffic as soon as possible. Investigations into the cause of the accident and follow-up actions are underway.

items.title: Price wars without efficiency boosts must come to an end
text: Imagine a crowded theater where one person stands up to get a better view. Soon, everyone follows suit, and the result is that everyone is standing, yet no one can see better than before. The only change is that watching the show has become more tiring.
This analogy aptly describes China's current debate over "involutionary" competition — a scenario where businesses continuously intensify their efforts without meaningful gains.

In recent months, regulators have stepped up scrutiny of subsidy-driven price wars among e-commerce platforms and penalized unfair competitive practices. The aim is not to stop companies from lowering prices but to prevent price cuts from becoming a contest that drains resources while doing little to improve products, services or productivity.

Low prices per se are not a problem. A new electric-vehicle maker may cut prices to enter the market or a retailer may offer discounts to clear inventory. Such strategies can benefit consumers and give new businesses a foothold. Competition is doing its job when lower prices reflect greater efficiency, better technology or a genuine effort to attract customers.

The problem begins when companies cut prices primarily because their rivals have done so. One company lowers its prices to protect market share, prompting others to follow suit to avoid losing customers. If none of the companies has a lasting cost advantage, the battle may leave their relative positions unchanged while shrinking profit margins across the industry. The market becomes busier, but not necessarily more productive.

This pattern has emerged in industries ranging from steel and cement to solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles. It has also taken hold in services such as delivery and ride-hailing, where platforms compete for users through discounts and subsidies. In some cases, opaque pricing practices and algorithmic tools make it harder for consumers and regulators to understand how prices are set. What looks like a bargain today may come at the expense of smaller merchants, sustainable business models or meaningful improvements in service.

The deeper problem is that some price wars can continue long after they become commercially untenable. A business that consistently sells below cost would normally have reason to rethink its strategy. But that calculation changes when losses are cushioned by preferential policies or other forms of external support.

Local governments have valid reasons to attract investment and foster industries suited to their economies. Yet, the pursuit of growth can become counterproductive when local officials compete to offer increasingly generous incentives, regardless of a project's commercial viability. One locality supports a favored industry; others respond with incentives of their own, hoping to keep investment and jobs at home. Companies gain room to maintain aggressive pricing, but the advantages may cancel each other out. Public funds are spent, fiscal pressures increase, and the underlying imbalance between supply and demand remains.

items.title: Keep geopolitics out of marine science
text: The politicization of marine scientific research is undermining the very cooperation needed to protect the oceans. Recently, some Philippine commentators have portrayed China's marine research activities near Huangyan Island and elsewhere in the South China Sea as potential "military threats". They have coined the term "ghost research ships", suggesting that routine scientific work is linked to military operations, submarine navigation and even anti-submarine warfare. By intertwining technological possibilities, the sensitivity of the locations and existing geopolitical tensions, they have crafted a narrative that misrepresents China's marine research as a "security concern". These claims lack supporting evidence and run counter to the international community's shared interest in advancing ocean science and protecting the marine environment.

Civic leader Jose Antonio Goitia repeatedly raises doubts about the identities of the Chinese vessels, equipment and purposes without providing conclusive evidence that they are engaged in military operations. This approach turns uncertainty into a perceived certainty of "threat". Instead of proving military engagement, it relies on insinuations and possibilities that lead the public to suspect that Chinese research vessels might be conducting military operations. Since each allegation is marked as unverified or under investigation, it cannot be refuted outright, allowing the negative perceptions to persist.

Official communication in the Philippines has further reinforced this narrative. Statements from the Philippine Coast Guard and military authorities have provided operational details and a broader security context, which, when combined with politically charged interpretations, blur the lines between facts and speculation. On Sept 28, the PCG linked anomalies in the Chinese research vessel Jia Hai Ke 7's automatic identification system signals to concerns about undersea communications cables and potential military data usage.

Similarly, on Oct 29, a PCG spokesperson speculated without any evidence that equipment on board an unidentified vessel near Huangyan Island might be a submersible or equipment for underwater operations, although its function had yet to be established. In subsequent coverage, the PCG's ongoing investigation appeared alongside Goitia's claims that autonomous underwater vehicles were being deployed to map submarine transit routes. This presentation risks leading readers to accept the speculative claims as confirmed facts.

items.title: Ministry of Commerce responds to US sanctions on 2 Chinese companies
text: China voiced firm opposition to the US decision to impose unilateral sanctions on two Chinese companies, the Ministry of Commerce said on Saturday, urging Washington to "promptly correct its wrongdoings".

On Thursday, the US State Department announced Cuba-related sanctions on China National Electronics Import & Export Corporation, an electronics and engineering company, and Beijing H&C Technologies Co Ltd, a security equipment supplier.

In a fact sheet, the department said the measures targeted "China-based suppliers of the regime's military forces" and alleged that the two companies had supplied components and equipment to Cuba's military through a Cuban procurement firm.

Imposing unilateral sanctions on Chinese companies on grounds involving a third party "violates international law and the basic norms governing international relations", a ministry spokesperson said in a statement.
The spokesperson added that Washington has recently stepped up sanctions and pressure on China, introducing a series of discriminatory restrictions in quick succession.

Such measures have seriously harmed the rights and interests of Chinese companies, the spokesperson said, adding that they run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and undermine the stability of bilateral economic and trade relations.
"China urges the United States to promptly correct its wrongful practices and reserves the right to take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests," the spokesperson said.

items.title: Start of Winter
Stephen Chao-An Chen: Connecting cultures through joy of learning
text: Language learning can encourage openness and connect people across cultures, said Stephen Chao-An Chen, general counsel of Duolingo, at the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit.

Describing the company's mission to make high-quality education universally accessible, Chen said its services reach 140 million people worldwide each month. He cited people learning French in China and Chinese in France as examples of the connections language learning creates.

Chen also highlighted engagement as a key to educational success. Characters such as Duo and Lily, alongside brand collaborations in China, help make learning appealing and encourage people to keep returning.

items.title: Xi casts ballot in Beijing's local legislative election
text: President Xi Jinping emphasized the need to practice whole-process people's democracy and ensure the election of deputies who meet the people's expectations, as he cast his ballot in a local people's congress election in Beijing on Friday.

Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, voted at the Huairentang polling station in the Zhongnanhai electoral district in Beijing's Xicheng district to elect deputies to the Xicheng district people's congress.

He underscored that electing people's congress deputies is the foundation for upholding, improving and effectively operating the people's congress system, and a major event in the country's political life.
Xi called for practicing whole-process people's democracy, upholding Party leadership, giving full play to democracy and acting in strict accordance with the law.

He also urged stronger oversight throughout the electoral process to ensure that elections proceed in the right direction and in a clean and upright atmosphere, and that the elected deputies meet the people's expectations.

The people's congress system is China's fundamental political system, with the National People's Congress serving as the supreme organ of State power. Deputies serve five-year terms, with voters directly electing representatives at the county and township levels. Deputies to people's congresses above the county level are elected by deputies at the next lower level.

On Friday afternoon, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi cast their ballots in person, while Han Zheng entrusted a staff member to vote on his behalf. Hu Jintao also entrusted a staff member to vote on his behalf.
Ballots were cast at 13,054 polling stations across Beijing to elect 4,898 new deputies to district-level people's congresses and 11,137 deputies to township-level people's congresses.

items.title: The path to constructive strategic stability | Short documentary | China-US relations
text: From Beijing in May to Washington in September, the Chinese and US presidents exchanged visits within six months, a pace unprecedented in bilateral relations.

At their May meeting, the two presidents agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. In September, they further developed that vision, agreeing to pursue "constructive strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity".

How did China navigate economic and trade tensions in Sino-US relations while keeping engagement on track? This Media Unlocked short documentary looks at the choices that helped move bilateral ties toward greater stability.

items.title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
text: As it expands its weather-warning systems across the Global South, China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU — an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration — to Sri Lanka, one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

The device, described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox, was presented to Sri Lanka’s meteorological department on Nov. 1. It will form part of a system designed to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year.

Launched in July 2025, MAZU takes its name from a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It combines AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from the country’s weather satellites.
Conventional weather forecasting relies on supercomputers to calculate how the atmosphere will change using equations based on physical laws. AI models, by contrast, learn from years of weather data.

“Chatbots familiar to the public learn patterns in language, while AI weather models learn how the atmosphere evolves,” Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led the development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, told Sixth Tone. “By training on years of meteorological data, these models can predict future weather conditions based on current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity.”

Once trained, AI models can produce forecasts faster and more cheaply than conventional methods. One model can generate a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods. For forecasts covering 15 to 60 days, AI models can reduce computing costs to one-thousandth of those of conventional methods.

But most of the savings come from running routine forecasts, Niu said. Training models, building datasets, and maintaining systems still require investment — resources many countries in the Global South lack.
MAZU’s cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, according to domestic media, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years.

In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data to develop warnings for heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods. In Djibouti, the model developed by Niu’s team helps provide tailored weather warnings for the East African country’s port.

Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, for which there is little historical data. Local weather in complex terrain also remains difficult to forecast, and it is not always clear how AI models arrive at their predictions.

The models also need to be adapted to local conditions, Niu said. “Our approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, conduct independent evaluations, and make local adjustments.”
Even with AI, he added, “human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings.”

items.title: China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019218/China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
text: Traditional Chinese colors have become a popular topic on Chinese social media, with posts sporting catchy headlines such as “Our Ancestors Had the Ultimate Eye for Beauty” and “Out-of-This-World Color Combinations in ‘Dream of the Red Chamber.’” Open one of these posts, and you’ll often find neatly arranged color swatches labeled with evocative traditional names such as tianqing, “celestial blue”; yuebai, “moon white”; qiuxiang, “autumn fragrance”; and yanzhi, “rouge.”

In my opinion, this enthusiasm is undoubtedly a good thing. Traditional colors deserve greater attention and should be made more accessible. Color swatches can also be useful for showcasing the colors of historical artifacts and help modern audiences connect with the past. But this kind of simplification is a double-edged sword. In making something rich and complex easier to understand, it can also reduce it to a crude, one-dimensional representation. What makes information easier to communicate can also obscure or distort its meaning.
In fact, color swatches have significant limitations when it comes to representing and explaining traditional colors. They can only scratch the surface of a much richer cultural history.

Modern color charts emerged from Western industrial and commercial systems designed to control production quality and reproduce specific colors. But this standardized, scientific approach often falls short when applied to traditional Chinese colors. Anyone who has visited an exhibition of antique clothing or textiles and tried to photograph it may have experienced this firsthand. What appears to the naked eye as a beautiful pine green might look mustard yellow on a smartphone screen. Or the various golds and yellows of an imperial dragon robe might lose their distinctiveness entirely. If even digital cameras equipped with sophisticated image-processing algorithms struggle to capture these colors, what chance does a simple color swatch have?
So why do modern industrial color charts fall short in representing traditional Chinese colors?

First, color swatches are designed to standardize colors within specific product categories, whereas traditional Chinese color names developed within particular craft traditions. As these traditions evolved, a color’s name could refer to subtly different hues in different periods.

Several factors contributed to these variations. In the age of traditional handicrafts, differences in materials and craftsmanship could produce markedly different hues. Local production conditions also gave products from different regions their own distinctive characteristics. Fashions changed over time, altering the shades associated with particular color names. Even on a single garment, colors could appear different depending on the lighting, viewing angle, or direction of the weave.

Traditional indigo dyeing offers a good example. Indigo must first be fermented in vats and chemically reduced before it can be used to dye fabric. A single dip produces a pale blue, and the color deepens after each subsequent immersion. As a result, even fabrics dyed in the same vat can emerge in countless different shades.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
text: Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang pledged to share China’s market with the rest of the world and promote balanced international economic development at the opening ceremony of the 2026 China International Import Expo (CIIE) on Thursday.
“Mutual benefit is at the heart of trade and economic cooperation,” Ding said in his opening address. “Open and connected markets are fundamental for such partnerships.”
Ding also called for deeper investment cooperation, greater collaboration in technological innovation, and stronger dialogue to remove trade barriers.

This year’s CIIE, the ninth annual event and the largest edition to date, welcomes a record 4,142 overseas companies from 162 countries, regions, and international organizations to Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center. The event’s total exhibition area is also its largest, exceeding 440,000 square meters.

The event, which runs Nov. 5 to 10, welcomed more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and global leading enterprises, with 2,000 companies participating for the first time. A record more than 480 products will either make their global, Asia, or China debut at the expo, including a laparoscopic surgery robot by Johnson & Johnson, a cochlear implant capable of 360-degree sound coverage by Swiss hearing care firm Advanced Bionics, and a 6G terminal prototype by U.S. tech company Qualcomm.

This year’s exhibition comprises six main sections covering technical equipment, consumer goods, food and agricultural products, automobiles and smart mobility, medical devices and health care, and trade in services. It also offers a dedicated “innovation incubation zone” for tech startups.

CIIE has also expanded efforts to support African countries, with free exhibition booth space for the “least developed” countries up 17% from last year’s exhibition. The expansion comes as China introduced zero tariffs on imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations in May.

Launched in 2018, CIIE is the world’s first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports. The expo underlines China’s continued efforts to promote inclusive economic globalization and build an open world economy.
In the first nine months of 2026, China’s imports of foreign goods reached 16.7 trillion yuan ($2.5 trillion), up 22.3% year on year, the fastest growth since 2021, according to official data.
(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo’s exhibition center in Shanghai, Nov. 5, 2026. VCG)

items.title: Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
text: Applications aimed at preventing impulse purchases have soared in popularity during this year’s Double Eleven, the world’s largest shopping festival. The apps involve users listing the items they want, along with their prices, then sharing them with friends and strangers who vote on whether they should buy them.

Dozens of such mini-programs have sprung up across major platforms including WeChat and Alipay following the August success of the WeChat mini-program “Still Want to Buy?” (Hai Mai Me in Chinese), domestic media reported last week. Related hashtags have garnered tens of millions of views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Thursday.

Domestic e-commerce giant Alibaba launched Double Eleven, also known as Singles’ Day, on Nov. 11, 2009, as a 24-hour shopping event. The festival has since grown to a monthlong event across all e-commerce platforms and begins around mid-October.

The trend comes as young Chinese consumers become increasingly money-conscious. According to a May report by Ireland-based consulting firm Accenture, 82% of the country’s Gen Z — more than 230 million people — have started saving money or cutting back on non-essential spending.

The rise in anti-impulse-buy apps dates back to the release of Still Want to Buy? in August. Created by a 29-year-old developer under the pseudonym Qiancheng, the app gained more than 75,000 daily active users within three days of its launch, and total registered users exceeded 500,000 as of mid-September. More than 85% of users are females under 24, Qiancheng told local media.

He said the tool came about after his girlfriend suggested using automated office purchase approval systems — which employees must go through to obtain authorization for work-related purchases — to govern shopping decisions. He added that he often personally feels regret after making impulse purchases.
“It’s difficult to make money nowadays, so I think it’s worth letting people we trust help us make better spending decisions,” Qiancheng said.

However, Still Want to Buy? was taken down on Oct. 31, reportedly due to targeted reporting from online trolls. Qiancheng told local media he is applying to have the mini-program relisted and is developing an independent app to expand the program’s function.
WeChat mini-program “Wait Up, Wallet” also offers similar features to Still Want to Buy?, but it allows users to seek advice from total strangers.

This October, Lin Yinjie, a 20-year-old college student from the eastern Fujian province, vibe-coded a similar app, the Alipay mini-program “Hold On a Sec.” The app lets users log items and prices and set a cooling-off period, during which friends help them decide whether to buy. So far, the program is mainly used by Lin and her friends and does not have a wide audience.

Lin told Sixth Tone that she used to place orders mindlessly while scrolling shopping apps and social media. “As a student on a tight budget, I know how easily the desire to buy things can quietly drain my wallet,” she said.

items.title: Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
text: For nearly 27 years, Starbucks coffeehouses in China have been a haven for non-paying patrons attracted by its comfortable seating, ample power outlets, air conditioning, and free restrooms.

This stemmed from the American company’s foundational brand concept of making its outlets “third places” — safe, accessible spaces between home and work to relax and connect with friends, whether you intend to spend or not.

In late October, Starbucks China introduced a nationwide purchase-required seating policy, pledging to be “clear in its rules but warm in its execution,” with staff encouraged to politely stop non-paying customers from hogging tables and chairs. At the same time, it unveiled plans to invest more than 300 million yuan ($45 million) in reshaping the in-store atmosphere.
As the company undergoes major corporate restructuring while continuing to expand, does it risk losing its “third place” image in China?
The first Starbucks on the Chinese mainland opened in Beijing’s World Trade Building in 1999. Today there are about 8,000 outlets across 1,100 counties in the mainland.

Li Kele regularly visits her local store in the southwestern Sichuan province. After walking in and sitting down on Oct. 21, taking a moment to browse various online platforms for discounts, Li was soon approached by a barista brandishing a menu and asking if she needed any help. “The store never used to push customers to place an order,” she says.
Starbucks outlets have been attracting non-paying patrons since the 1980s, and the company officially adopted a worldwide open-door policy in 2018.

However, concerns over disruptive behaviors, alongside the company’s desire to prioritize paying customers and staff’s experience, prompted the global headquarters to reverse the policy in January last year.
The change began at its North American stores, where a new code of conduct stated that Starbucks coffee shops, patios, restrooms, and other facilities were for employees and customers only.
Anecdotal evidence suggests baristas in China began nudging seated patrons to make purchases in early 2026.

One customer shares that in January they observed employees at a Starbucks branch in Beijing’s central Xidan shopping district walking around the store offering table service to people without drinks, which is not typically available, and promoting discount coupons. Sometimes they’d subtly point out that the store was crowded and seating was scarce.
On Oct. 19, social media users in several cities began posting about signs spotted at Starbucks stores that stated customers should “make a purchase before taking a seat.”

When a domestic media outlet contacted Starbucks China for a response that same day, a spokesperson denied any plan to introduce a purchase-required seating policy. But within 48 hours, the company made a complete U-turn, announcing that such a policy would take effect on Oct. 22.
The move has sparked much debate online. Yet in real terms, implementation has so far been limited to advisory measures, such as signage.

items.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
text: A Chinese app designed to report hotels that allegedly have bedbugs and other pests has been updated and re-released following controversy over the validity of the claims. The app attracted more than 300,000 users at its peak, flagging over 600 hotels nationwide, according to its creator.

In a Sunday post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, the creator of the app, a WeChat mini-program called “Bedbug Map,” announced that he alone would now review bedbug reports — previously, evidence was approved if a majority of users verified it. He also clarified that users are required to upload photographic evidence of bedbugs. The next day, he also posted a review of nearly 300 rejected bedbug reports, explaining why each had been declined.

Released Sept. 16, the mini-program lets users report hotels with bedbugs, cockroaches, or other pests, resulting in a bug or question mark icon over the hotel’s location. Tapping it reveals the number of user reports.

Controversy arose after reports that multiple hotels were asked by customers for refunds after they reported having found bedbugs via the app after their stay. One hotel was allegedly asked to refund 3,000 yuan ($450) in room charges after a report citing “two bumps” on a guest’s body was posted on the map and approved by users. According to the report, the hotel later asked a third party to inspect the premises, but found no traces of bedbugs.

The creator, a 26-year-old manufacturing industry worker who asked to remain anonymous, told Sixth Tone that in the past few days he had personally reviewed more than 700 pieces of photo evidence submitted over the previous two months.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone revealed that 232 hotels are now marked on the mini-program’s map, down from the more than 600 reported before Monday. The mini-program currently lists 36 hotels as having successfully appealed reports after submitting third-party evidence.
The app has also been taken down twice, most recently in late October, by WeChat parent company Tencent, citing its restrictions on applications run by and registered to individuals.

The creator told Sixth Tone that Bedbug Map was created with the help of AI in under two weeks. He said he got the idea after searching online for bedbug information after he and his girlfriend developed bites following a move, discovering most bedbug posts involved hotels.

On the day of its release, the mini-program attracted over 100,000 users, according to the creator. Under his release announcement on Xiaohongshu, many commented asking him to expand the function to public transportation, which he then added to the app. However, the function was removed in subsequent updates.
“I guess the reason the app was well-received is that it addresses a key pain point for the average traveler: the lack of cleanliness and the resurgence of bedbugs.”

items.title: Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
text: A few weeks ago, I served as a judge on a food program in China, where I met many chefs and got a close look at how they develop new dishes. I was particularly impressed by one dish: a steamed egg custard topped with a rich crab paste made from crab roe and fat. It was a combination I had never considered before. The crab paste had a delicate aroma and a rich, oily texture, while the steamed egg custard was soft and silky, perfectly balancing its richness.
I was struck by the dish’s ingenuity, but it also raised a question: Would people be willing to pay for the recipe and instructions on how to make it?

I put this question to one of the chefs on the program. He smiled at me as though I were a child and asked why anyone would pay for a recipe. He then let me in on an industry secret: When a restaurant discovers that a competitor has introduced a new dish, it will order it and have its own chefs taste it, analyze its ingredients, cooking techniques, and seasonings, and work out how it was made. In most cases, they can reproduce it. The chef told me he had recreated other people’s dishes and had his own copied by others.
It all sounded rather cutthroat. The person who bears the cost of innovation often reaps little of the reward.

In Chinese cuisine, creating a new dish is not nearly as simple as diners might imagine. Chefs must find the right ingredients, adjust proportions, experiment with different cooking temperatures, refine textures, and continually adjust based on customer feedback. Developing a successful dish can involve dozens or even hundreds of failed attempts before it is ready to serve.

The time, ingredients, and labor costs of this trial-and-error process are all borne by the original creator. Yet as soon as the dish reaches the table, anyone can observe, taste, analyze, and even reproduce it. For a competitor, learning most of the techniques needed to make a dish may cost little more than the price of a meal.

Even more frustrating, many of these innovators lack the resources to promote their creations. A small restaurant might be the first to develop a dish but lack the advertising budget, media exposure, or network of locations to popularize it. Meanwhile, a larger restaurant can simply copy the dish and quickly introduce it to a wider audience. Since more people encounter it there first, they may assume the larger restaurant came up with it.

This suggests that the first-mover advantage does not necessarily apply in the restaurant business. Being first matters only if consumers know who created the dish and the original creator has the resources and business acumen to turn that innovation into a brand and a source of revenue. Otherwise, the creator is essentially providing free research and development while introducing consumers to a dish that benefits the entire market.

items.title: China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
text: China has approved its first domestically developed amino acid-based nutritional powder, designed to give patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) — a rare genetic disorder that affects metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine — greater freedom in what they eat. Treatment of PKU requires lifelong dietary restrictions to prevent developmental disorders and brain damage.

The new formula officially entered the Chinese market on Oct. 30 and was jointly developed by Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research, and dairy producer Bright Dairy.
PKU affects about one in every 11,000 newborns in China, with an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 registered patients nationwide.

Due to a genetic defect, people with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. The resulting buildup can damage brain cells, requiring patients to follow a low-phenylalanine diet by cutting out meat and eating low-protein grains, while relying on milk powder-like formulas to supplement the other amino acids they need.
Earlier formulas contained 30% to 60% amino acids, with the rest composed of fats, carbohydrates, and other nutrients.

“As patients grow older, they need more protein. That means consuming more of these formulas, which also means taking in more fats and carbohydrates, increasing the risk of obesity,” Cai Wei, director of the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research and leader of the research team, told domestic media.

In contrast, the new formula contains 95% amino acids, allowing patients to meet their amino acid needs without consuming as much fat or as many carbohydrates, and giving them more freedom to enjoy other normal low-protein foods.

Zhuang Yingying, a 33-year-old PKU patient, told domestic media that patients previously relied heavily on imported products, and overseas supply disruptions were common. Special low-protein foods such as rice and noodles cost five to 10 times as much as regular varieties.
The formula, designed for PKU patients aged 1 and older, could save some families more than 1,000 yuan ($140) a month, according to domestic media.

Domestic PKU formulas have existed for decades, but long faced hurdles in gaining regulatory approval in China, partly because of gaps in national standards for food-grade amino acids, according to a 2020 report by domestic media outlet China Times. High registration costs and the small patient population have also discouraged manufacturers from entering the market.
China approved its first PKU medical formula in 2018, an imported product, while the first domestically produced formula received regulatory approval in 2025.

Since 2018, some parts of China, including Shanghai and neighboring Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, have introduced public health insurance coverage for foods formulated for PKU patients. In Shanghai, annual coverage ranges from 8,000 yuan for infants under 1 to 12,000 yuan for patients over 10.

items.title: Annual CIIE opens in Shanghai, showcasing China's commitment to opening up
text: On Thursday morning, in the waiting lounge of the opening ceremony of the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, two hours before the ceremony began, the guests had already begun arriving.

They took selfies, chatted, posed for group photos with old friends and gave interviews to the media. According to on-site observations by the Global Times, in the relaxing atmosphere, the words they mentioned most were "opportunity", "openness" and "market."

Running from Thursday to Tuesday next week, this year's CIIE has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors, with total exhibition area exceeding 440,000 square meters. Over 480 exhibits are set to make their global, Asian or China debut at the event, the highest number in history. In addition, nearly 200 companies and institutions have been "full attendees" at the CIIE for all nine editions.

In his keynote speech at the opening ceremony, Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said that the CIIE has witnessed China's firm determination and concrete actions to promote high-standard opening-up, the remarkable results and tremendous gains of businesses and people from various countries in sharing opportunities in the Chinese market, and the unremitting efforts and important contributions of visionary people from all walks of life in improving global economic governance, according to Xinhua News Agency.

This fully demonstrates China's strategic resolve in advancing high-standard opening-up, injecting valuable certainty, stability and confidence in development into the world, Hu Qimu, professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Thursday.

Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker of Austria, and UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo attended the opening ceremony and delivered remarks, Xinhua reported.

Ding's speech was welcomed by many executives from global multinational companies, who said they draw great inspiration from the speech and remain confident in honoring their long-term commitment to China.

Rogier Janssens, President of Merck China, told the Global Times that CIIE brings the world to China, and gives China a stronger voice in the global conversation. "As China moves into its 15th Five-Year Plan, the Expo's role is even more important," Janssens said.

The CIIE opening ceremony underscored the importance of openness, collaboration and innovation-driven development, further reinforcing Henkel's confidence in the long-term growth of the Chinese market, Anna An, President of Henkel China told the Global Times on Thursday.

Vice Premier Ding's speech reaffirmed China's steadfast commitment to high-standard opening-up and highlighted the country's important role in driving growth and building an open global economy, echoed Poh-Yian Koh, President of FedEx China.

items.title: Recalibrating the world's cognitive coordinates
text: In September 2026, the Global South moved to recalibrate the world's old cognitive coordinate system at three levels: institutions, initiatives and public discourse.

At the institutional level, on Sept. 4, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution on "correcting the map" by a vote of 164 to 1, encouraging the replacement of the Mercator projection, which inflates high latitudes and compresses the equator, with the Equal Earth projection. The United States cast the sole opposing vote.

At the level of initiatives, on Sept. 12-13, BRICS leaders issued a declaration in New Delhi explicitly calling for international law and international rules to be "applied equally, without double standards."

At the level of public discourse, from Sept. 22 to 28, the General Debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly was held at UN Headquarters in New York. From Nairobi to Belgrade, leaders took turns criticizing the same thing: international law is being applied selectively.

From the projection of a map to the scale on which a rule is applied and then the authority to interpret an order, the domains differ and the levels differ, but the question being asked was the same: Who sets the world's cognitive coordinates?

This recalibration first took place on the map. The Mercator projection was born in the Age of Exploration as a technical tool for ocean navigation. It accurately represents direction and routes, but systematically distorts area.

Over the centuries, the navigation chart made its way into textbooks and newspaper pages, and eventually became what people took to be "the world itself." A technical choice originally made for navigation thus quietly became the default framework through which people perceived the world.

In this projection, the higher the latitude, the more it is magnified. Europe and North America accordingly sit at the top of the map, while regions in the equatorial belt, such as Africa and Latin America, are compressed. Greenland looks nearly as big as Africa on the map, yet Africa's actual land area is 14 times the size of Greenland.
The African Union notes that the world's long-standing perception of Africa rests on a distorted map. The UN General Assembly resolution therefore means far more than a technical fix to map-making.

It does not require the Mercator projection to withdraw from navigation and aviation, nor should it. What it challenges is the monopoly of the "default base map": When public communication needs to show the true size and position of countries, it cannot continue to present a base map that magnifies the few and compresses the many as if it were the world as it actually is.

At the same time, correcting a bias is not about replacing one bias with another, such as drawing a map that elevates the South, but about acknowledging that every projection involves trade-offs. The question is which set of trade-offs has been treated as the only standard.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: 2026 World Ocean Week spotlights China's ocean governance role
text: The 2026 World Ocean Week opened on November 5 in Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province, unveiling five outcomes, including a publication on seamounts and a dedicated ecological and environmental data product.

The week also features 33 activities, including seminars on marine science and ecology and industry and business matchmaking events, to advance global ocean governance and the high-quality development of the blue economy.

A bilingual report on the status, role and prospects of the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), and China's role in it, was released on the same day.

Compiled by the China Institute for Marine Development Strategy under the Ministry of Natural Resources, the report outlines the significance of the agreement's entry into force and China's contributions to its negotiation and implementation.

The BBNJ Agreement took effect on January 17, 2026, becoming the third implementing agreement to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and filling a legal gap in the conservation and governance of marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

China participated in nearly 20 years of negotiations and put forward proposals on the agreement's four key areas. Its contributions included promoting a benefit-sharing mechanism for marine genetic resources, advancing area-based management tools, improving transparency in environmental impact assessments and helping developing countries build capacity to implement the agreement.

China has designated marine ecological conservation redlines covering about 150,000 square kilometers, established 353 marine protected areas and carried out 194 marine ecological conservation projects. It is also one of the few countries worldwide to have recorded a net increase in mangrove area.

China has made manned deep-sea submersibles Jiaolong and Fendouzhe, as well as research vessels such as Deep Sea No. 1, available for international scientific expeditions. It preserves nearly 60,000 marine microbial resources and provides international users with access to samples and data.

Under the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development, China has led 10 major international science programs, including one on the digital discovery of typical deep-sea habitats.

China has improved its legal framework for environmental impact assessments of activities in the international seabed area, while contractors engaged in mineral exploration there have actively fulfilled their assessment obligations.
Its experience, environmental data, expertise, and trained personnel can help developing countries assess deep-sea activities and promote a greener, low-carbon approach to ocean activities.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Computing-Electricity Index offers a precise portrait of China's computing power industry
text: Staff members from State Grid Hangzhou Power Supply Company visited China Mobile (Hangzhou) Information Technology Co., Ltd. on November 2, delivering a customized computing operations monitoring report built on a Computing-Electricity Index system. Based on the company's electricity consumption, the team also conducted on-site load analysis, energy efficiency assessment and electricity-use advisory services.

The report covers data center cabinet load rates, server rack deployment rates, green electricity consumption, and rack energy efficiency, offering a clear picture of a company's computing operations and electricity use.

Like a dedicated "health checkup report," it provides a reference for companies to assess the performance of their computing operations, optimize operations and management, and develop expansion plans.

"The Computing-Electricity Index shows that our intelligent computing business is growing rapidly and demand for high-end computing is strong. It recommends that newly added computing capacity be prioritized for intelligent computing and AI inference scenariosputing capacity be prioritized for intelligent computing and A" said the head of the company's data center.

The Computing-Electricity Index uses big power data as its foundation to quantify and score the prosperity of the computing power industry across four dimensions: scale momentum, business climate, expected vitality and green efficiency. The index system consists of two scale-momentum indicators, three business-climate indicators, two future-vitality indicators and two green-efficiency indicators. It can support the government in coordinating computing and power resources, while also providing a basis for enterprises to expand computing capacity, save energy and reduce carbon emissions.

Guided by the index's monitoring results, State Grid Hangzhou Power Supply Company is extending its power services beyond support for individual projects to serve the development of the computing power industry, taking a more proactive approach to service delivery.

Given computing power enterprises' large electricity capacity requirements, rapid load growth and high requirements for power supply reliability, the company has strengthened load monitoring and trend analysis for computing centers, promptly detecting abnormal load fluctuations and providing early warnings on risks related to energy efficiency and power quality.

For key computing projects, it implements list-based management and forms "1+N" service teams to provide contracted power connection services and customized power supply plans, while delivering targeted power supply support based on each enterprise's electricity-use sensitivity level.

items.title: China's services trade rises 8.5% in first nine months of 2026, deficit narrows
text: China's services trade grew 8.5 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, with the trade deficit narrowing and transport services leading growth, official data showed on Wednesday, as the country steps up efforts to foster new growth drivers in the services sector.

The sustained expansion reflects a broader shift toward higher-value services, as China's vast manufacturing base and industrial upgrading open new opportunities in international markets and deepen the integration of manufacturing and modern services, analysts said.

According to the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM), China's services trade reached 5.77 trillion yuan ($863.7 billion) during the January-September period. Exports rose 14.8 percent to 2.27 trillion yuan, outpacing a 4.8 percent increase in imports. The services trade deficit narrowed by 132.66 billion yuan from a year earlier to 1.23 trillion yuan.

Transport services led all categories in trade growth, with combined imports and exports surging 33.9 percent to 1.28 trillion yuan, making it China's third-largest services trade category after travel and other business services.

Knowledge-intensive services also maintained solid growth. Trade in the category rose 7.4 percent in the first nine months. Exports climbed 11.7 percent to 1.22 trillion yuan, making up 53.7 percent of total services exports. Personal, cultural and recreational services posted the fastest rate of export growth at 69.1 percent, followed by insurance and pension services at 50.3 percent.

Song Ding, a senior research fellow at the Shenzhen-based China Development Institute, described the narrowing trade deficit as an encouraging development, pointing to China's growing services export capacity and international competitiveness.

"When manufacturing reaches a certain level of development, especially on the scale seen in China, moving further up the value chain and expanding into modern services becomes a natural progression," Song told the Global Times on Wednesday.
This shift is also evident in the growing links between China's manufacturing exports and international transport services, Song said.

"As Chinese-made goods reach more overseas markets, domestic companies are expanding their presence in shipping, rail freight and air cargo networks, rather than relying solely on foreign operators to handle international deliveries."

The momentum is also evident in China's broader services sector. China's services sector expanded 5.2 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters, outpacing overall GDP growth of 4.6 percent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). The sector contributed 66.3 percent of economic growth, up 5.6 percentage points from a year earlier.

At an October 19 press briefing, NBS Deputy Commissioner Mao Shengyong highlighted the accelerating integration of advanced manufacturing and modern services, with industrial chains moving toward more specialized, higher-value activities. He also identified artificial intelligence as a key driver of growth in the information technology-related sector.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Chinese consulate demands justice after delivery worker killed in Melbourne
text: The tragedy has sparked online outrage over delivery platform policies and gig worker safety

A 47-year-old delivery man from China’s northwestern Shaanxi province was stabbed to death while on the job and another rider was injured in downtown Melbourne on Friday evening, after the two confronted a man who was “tampering” with their bikes, sparking an “altercation”, Victoria state police said.
A 51-year-old suspect was arrested on Saturday morning and remains in custody, while the second delivery rider was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening stab wounds, according to police.

items.title: Pakistani astronaut to join China’s next space station mission
text: China’s Manned Space Agency has selected a Pakistani astronaut as a payload specialist for its upcoming Shenzhou-24 mission, making the unnamed individual the first foreign national to visit the country’s space station.
The Pakistani astronaut would join China’s Shenzhou-24 mission, as part of bilateral cooperation under Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, Chinese state media reported on Saturday.
China has not identified the astronaut nor given a date of departure, but the mission is expected to take place by the end of the year.
Pakistani pilots Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud spent months training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Center in Beijing for a mission.

Last February, Pakistan and China, longstanding strategic and diplomatic partners, entered into an agreement, establishing a Chinese government-led programme to train Pakistani astronauts. China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a key foreign investor.

The China National Space Administration will also deploy Jinnah-1, Pakistan’s inaugural lunar rover. Weighing 35kg (77lb) and fitted with specialised scientific equipment, the rover is tasked with analysing plasma behaviour, radiation, and the composition of lunar soil.
The training programme includes practical operational exercises and intensive Chinese language lessons to prepare the candidates for the mission.
Beijing’s China Central Television reported that after completing a short-term in-orbit flight, the astronauts would return to Earth on board the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.
China invested heavily in its space programme in recent years – catching up with its main rival, the United States – and aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030.

The US, Russia, and China are also racing to build nuclear reactors on the Moon. While the US space agency, NASA, announced plans to develop a nuclear reactor on the Moon by the end of 2030, Russia has been working with China and aims to do the same by 2036.

The reactors will be needed to power the mining of frozen water trapped deep in the moon’s craters, which scientists believe could supply drinking water, air, and rocket fuel for future bases. The reactors would also provide power for lunar bases.

US asks China to uphold Busan trade deal commitments ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
text: Top officials of United States President Donald Trump's administration have called on China to "fully and immediately" implement its commitments under a 2025 trade agreement between the two nations, including on rare earth and other critical minerals.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Friday held a videoconference with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on the trade and economic relationship between Washington and Beijing, a statement from Greer's office said.

Greer "emphasized the critical importance of China taking concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals.” it added.

The US officials were referring to an accord reached between the world's two largest economies in 2025 in a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in South Korea's Busan, on the sidelines of  an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
The deal had been reached during a period that saw the two countries exchange tariff escalations prompted by Trump's wider tariffs policy, which particularly targeted China, among other countries.
The accord capped US tariffs on Chinese goods —  enforced during Trump's second stint as president —  at about 20%.
China agreed to buy 25 million metric tons of US soybeans for the next three years.
Beijing also said it would keep China's rare earth exports flowing, suspending new export curbs.
The minerals are critical for the technological industry, and the Trump administration has in the past complained that Beijing was not meeting its commitments regarding supply.

"The Trump Administration will continue pursuing policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen our economic and national security,” Bessent wrote on X after the high-level call.

He, who is Beijing's lead negotiator on trade ties with the US, during Friday's interaction expressed  "serious concern" over recent US trade restrictions targeting his country, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
The report did not elaborate which measure the vice premier was referring to.
But both parties agreed to "continuously strengthen cooperation”and "properly manage differences" to promote a "stable" US-China trade relationship, Xinhua said.
The Busan trade deal  at first covered only one year, but the US and China extended their trade pact until January 10 next year, as  Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September.
The two leaders are expected to meet again at the upcoming APEC forum in Shenzhen, China, slated from November 18 to 19.

Meanwhile, in a separate development, China has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a historic trilateral summit of Xi, Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC gathering.

China "is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry, said at a media briefing in Beijing this week.

On Thursday, Unesco released this year’s nominations for inclusion on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The 59 nominations submitted for consideration for the UN cultural body’s list include Chinese cuisine, Spain’s traditional jota music and dance genre, and Japan’s shodo calligraphy.
